transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Yeah… I guess what brings me in is, I just don’t want to do the things that usually keep me going anymore. Like salsa nights — I used to love those, even if I wasn’t the best dancer. And church gatherings, cooking something for the neighbors… I used to do that without thinking.

Even walking into my shop, you know, just to smell the wood and be around my tools — that used to settle me. Now I don’t even feel like doing that. It’s like the wanting part got shut off.
Did something stressful happen in your life shortly before this started?

Yeah… yeah, something did. My wife’s health kind of suddenly went downhill, about two months ago, and everything in our routine changed after that.

I mean, we had our ways of doing things — little things, like who made coffee, when I’d open the shop, what days we’d go by church — and then all of a sudden it wasn’t like that anymore. Funny how you don’t think a routine matters until it’s gone. But yeah, that’s when this whole change in me started, around then.
When you have a bad day emotionally, is it mostly because you’re thinking about your wife’s illness and how life has changed?

Yeah… mostly, yeah. It’s not just sadness about her being sick, though. I get stuck going back over everything — every appointment, every little change in how she was doing — and I start thinking, you know, if I’d been paying better attention maybe I would’ve caught something sooner.

I know I’m not a doctor. I know that. I build cabinets and repair doorframes and all that… I’ve spent half my life noticing when a board is warped before anybody else sees it. So then I think, how did I not notice this? A better husband would’ve protected her somehow. That’s where my mind goes on the bad days.
Even when you’re not thinking about your wife’s illness, do you still feel down or unable to enjoy things?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, the thoughts about my wife make it worse, no question, but even when I’m not sitting there thinking on it, I still don’t really want to do anything.

Like salsa night — I used to go even if I came home with sore knees, and I’d laugh about it. Or church gatherings, cooking a tray of something for the neighbors… those things used to fill me up. Even the shop, just walking in and smelling the wood, seeing the tools where I left them — that used to be enough to get me moving.

Now I’ll stand there and it’s like… nothing catches. Like the wanting part of me isn’t there.
Aside from losing interest in things, have you been feeling sad or down most days?

Yeah… yes, most days. Especially mornings. I wake up and before I even get out of bed there’s this heavy, empty feeling right here in my chest.

It’s strange, because the house can look the same — same curtains, same dishes in the sink, same little creak in the hallway floor I’ve been meaning to fix for years — but it feels like the color’s gone out of it. Like everything’s dimmer.

And I try not to show it too much in front of my wife. I’ll go make coffee or fuss with something in the kitchen just so I don’t break down where she can see me. But yeah… sad, down, whatever word fits. Most days.
If your wife’s health had not changed, do you think you would still be feeling this down?

I don’t know… I mean, it’s hard to separate it, because her health is woven into everything now. Like even making breakfast, I’m looking at the chair she sits in, or the cup she likes, and my mind goes there.

But… I think I’d still be down. Maybe not in the exact same way, but most mornings I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest before anything even happens. The house feels like the color’s gone out of it, you know? And I have to force myself to get moving, to not break down in front of her.

I wish I could say it’s only because of what happened with her, but it feels bigger than that sometimes.
Before your wife became ill, had you been feeling down like this for years?

No… not for years, not like this. I mean, I’ve had rough patches before — everybody does, right? Work slows down, bills pile up, you throw your back out lifting something you knew you shouldn’t have lifted… I can get gloomy.

But this… this has been more like, I don’t know, about six months now? Dragging on long enough that it doesn’t feel like just a bad week or regular stress. It’s settled in more than I’m used to.
Before your wife became ill, was there ever another time in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

I’m not sure… I’m trying to think. There were times I was low, sure. Life has a way of doing that to you. I remember one winter when work was slow and I kept staring at the phone waiting for jobs to come in, and I’d go out to the garage just to move lumber around like that was going to fix anything.

But depressed like this… for two weeks or more… I don’t know if I can say that. I’m not sure I’ve kept track of it that way. Things kind of blur together when you’re just trying to get through the day, you know?
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, not just your wife’s health?

I don’t know… I mean, I worry, sure. Who doesn’t? There’s always something — the truck making that noise, whether I measured a cut wrong, bills showing up right when you think you’ve got a little breathing room.

But many different things… I’m not sure. My mind does wander all over the place sometimes. Like yesterday I went out to the garage to look for a screwdriver and ended up sorting through this old coffee can full of bent nails my dad would’ve thrown a fit about me keeping. He used to say, “A clean shop is a safe shop,” and mine’s never been either one.

Sorry… I’m getting off track. I guess I’m not sure how much of it is worry versus just thoughts bouncing around.
Before this current stretch, was there ever a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m trying to pin that down, but I honestly don’t know. I’ve had spells where I didn’t feel like doing much, where the shop just felt cold and the tools sat there, you know… and I’d tell myself I was just tired or work was slow.

But nearly every day for two weeks… before this? I can’t say for sure. I never marked it on a calendar or anything. Things sort of run together after a while.
Have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty lately?

Yeah… I have. More than I probably want to admit.

I keep going back over every appointment, every time my wife seemed a little different, every little change in her health, and I think… why didn’t I catch that? A better husband would’ve noticed sooner, or pushed harder, or protected her somehow. I know that sounds— I don’t know, maybe it doesn’t make sense.

It’s like when you’re building stairs and one measurement is off early, everything after that is off too. I keep thinking I missed the measurement. Like it’s on me somehow.
Have you noticed a change in your sleep lately?

Sleep… I don’t know. I mean, it’s not like I’ve been keeping track of it.

Some nights I’m in bed and I feel like I must’ve slept, because the clock’s moved, but it doesn’t feel like much. Other nights I’m just… thinking. Then I get annoyed at the sheets, or the room feels too quiet, and I start wondering if I should fix that loose hinge on the closet door because it catches every time you open it.

But has it changed? I’m not sure. Maybe. I couldn’t say exactly.
Before this current period, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly.

There were times before where I got pretty low, or I stopped wanting to do things I usually cared about, but whether it was nearly every day for two full weeks… I can’t swear to that. I wasn’t exactly taking notes. I’d just go to work, come home, maybe sit in the garage awhile pretending I was going to sharpen something or fix something, and then not really do it.

But that could’ve been a few days, or a week, or longer. Time gets funny when you’re just getting through it. So… I’m not saying no, I just can’t give you a solid yes either.
Before this current period, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yeah… I mean, before this, I don’t know if I could put a calendar around it and say “that was exactly two weeks,” you know?

But the feeling itself—yeah. Most mornings I’d wake up and there’d be this heavy, empty feeling right here in my chest. Like the whole house had the color drained out of it. And I’d have to sort of… brace myself before getting up, because I didn’t want my wife to see me fall apart.

It’s funny, not funny, but morning light used to tell me what needed fixing—trim, paint, whatever—and then it just started feeling like another thing I had to get through. So… yes, I think there were stretches like that, even if I can’t pin down the exact length.
Before this current period, was there ever a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, that’s kind of what got me here, if I’m being honest.

It’s not just “sad,” exactly. It’s more like the things that usually keep me going just don’t pull me anymore. Salsa nights, for one—I used to like that, even if I wasn’t the best dancer in the room. Church gatherings too, cooking something for the neighbors… I used to make this big pot of beans sometimes, and people would come by after, you know, just talking in the driveway.

And my shop… that’s the one that bothers me. I used to walk in there just to smell the wood, even if I wasn’t building anything. Now I don’t even want to go in. So, yeah, I guess there have been times like that, nearly every day, where I just stopped wanting any of it.
Do your low mood and loss of interest ever come on even when nothing about your wife’s illness is on your mind?

Yeah… sometimes it’s not like I’m actively thinking about her being sick.

I’ll wake up and it’s just there already, before I’ve even had a proper thought about anything. This heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like the house has gone flat somehow, like all the color’s been drained out of it.

And then I’m lying there trying to get myself together before she notices—because I don’t want to break down in front of her. I’ll start thinking, well, maybe I should fix that loose hinge or check the back steps, but it’s not really about the hinge. It’s just… the morning hits me that way sometimes, whether I’ve been thinking about her illness or not.
Before this current period, was there ever a separate time in your life when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yeah… separate from now, yes, I think there was. I know I keep circling around it, but the mornings are what I remember most.

I’d wake up and before I even had my feet on the floor, there’d be this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like someone had taken all the color out of the house. And I’d just lie there trying to pull myself together, because I didn’t want my wife to see me break down.

It wasn’t just one bad morning, either. It was… most mornings, day after day. I’m not great with exact dates, but it felt like it went on long enough that it wasn’t just a rough patch.
Before this current period, was there another separate time in your life when you felt this same kind of depression for at least two weeks?

Yeah… I mean, I think so. It’s hard to separate them out cleanly, because after a while all those mornings kind of run together.

But there was another stretch where most mornings I’d wake up and it was already there—this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like the house had lost all its color. I’d just lie there a bit, listening to the pipes or the birds outside, thinking I should get up and do something useful… and instead I’d be trying not to fall apart before my wife saw me.

So, yeah. It wasn’t just a day or two. It went on long enough that I’d say it was at least a couple weeks.
Have you noticed a change in your appetite lately?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I eat, but I don’t know that I’ve been paying close attention to it.

Some days I’ll stand in the kitchen and open the fridge and forget what I was even looking for, then notice that little catch on the door still sticks—been meaning to plane it down, just haven’t. My wife will ask if I want something and I’ll say “yeah, sure,” but I couldn’t tell you if I’m hungrier or less hungry than usual.

So… I don’t know. Nothing I’ve clearly noticed, I guess.
Has this been making it hard for you to keep up with your work in the shop?

Yeah… it has. More than I like to admit.

In the shop, I’ve had to hand off parts of jobs I’d normally keep an eye on myself. I’ve always been pretty particular about that—measure twice, make sure the trim lines up right, the little stuff people don’t notice unless it’s wrong. But lately I just… I can’t seem to stay on top of all of it.

And it’s not just work, I guess. I’ve kind of pulled back from people too—church, friends, the neighbors. My wife noticed, and even someone from the parish got worried enough to check in about whether I was safe. That was… embarrassing. But yeah, it’s been affecting things.

doctor.question: Before this current period, was there ever a time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, that’s kind of what got me here, if I’m being honest.

It’s not just “sad,” exactly. It’s more like the things that usually keep me going just don’t pull me anymore. Salsa nights, for one—I used to like that, even if I wasn’t the best dancer in the room. Church gatherings too, cooking something for the neighbors… I used to make this big pot of beans sometimes, and people would come by after, you know, just talking in the driveway.

And my shop… that’s the one that bothers me. I used to walk in there just to smell the wood, even if I wasn’t building anything. Now I don’t even want to go in. So, yeah, I guess there have been times like that, nearly every day, where I just stopped wanting any of it.

Yeah… sometimes it’s not like I’m actively thinking about her being sick.

I’ll wake up and it’s just there already, before I’ve even had a proper thought about anything. This heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like the house has gone flat somehow, like all the color’s been drained out of it.

And then I’m lying there trying to get myself together before she notices—because I don’t want to break down in front of her. I’ll start thinking, well, maybe I should fix that loose hinge or check the back steps, but it’s not really about the hinge. It’s just… the morning hits me that way sometimes, whether I’ve been thinking about her illness or not.

I’d wake up and before I even had my feet on the floor, there’d be this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like someone had taken all the color out of the house. And I’d just lie there trying to pull myself together, because I didn’t want my wife to see me break down.

doctor.question: Before this current period, was there another separate time in your life when you felt this same kind of depression for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood

Yeah… I mean, I think so. It’s hard to separate them out cleanly, because after a while all those mornings kind of run together.

But there was another stretch where most mornings I’d wake up and it was already there—this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Like the house had lost all its color. I’d just lie there a bit, listening to the pipes or the birds outside, thinking I should get up and do something useful… and instead I’d be trying not to fall apart before my wife saw me.

So, yeah. It wasn’t just a day or two. It went on long enough that I’d say it was at least a couple weeks.

Some days I’ll stand in the kitchen and open the fridge and forget what I was even looking for, then notice that little catch on the door still sticks—been meaning to plane it down, just haven’t. My wife will ask if I want something and I’ll say “yeah, sure,” but I couldn’t tell you if I’m hungrier or less hungry than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode causes significant functional impairment, which helps distinguish major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder or generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Has this been making it hard for you to keep up with your work in the shop?

patient.answer:
Yeah… it has. More than I like to admit.

In the shop, I’ve had to hand off parts of jobs I’d normally keep an eye on myself. I’ve always been pretty particular about that—measure twice, make sure the trim lines up right, the little stuff people don’t notice unless it’s wrong. But lately I just… I can’t seem to stay on top of all of it.

And it’s not just work, I guess. I’ve kind of pulled back from people too—church, friends, the neighbors. My wife noticed, and even someone from the parish got worried enough to check in about whether I was safe. That was… embarrassing. But yeah, it’s been affecting things.
